title: Why Your Voice Sounds So Weird on Recordings
description:
Does your recorded voice make you cringe? Here's why it sounds like a stranger.

When you talk, you hear yourself two ways: through the air AND through vibrations in your skull that reach your inner ear directly. Your head boosts the low frequencies, so to you, your voice sounds deeper and fuller. A recording only captures the air version, the one everyone else hears.

The twist: in a 2013 study (Hughes & Harrison, Perception), people rated voice clips without knowing their own voice was mixed in, and rated their own voice as more attractive than others did and more than other people's voices.

Would you recognize your own voice in a blind test? 👇

Sources:
- Scientific American, Why does my voice sound so different when it is recorded and played back? (Timothy Hullar, Washington University School of Medicine): https://scientificamerican.com/article/why-does-my-voice-sound-different
- Popular Science, Why your voice sounds different on recordings (Ben Hornsby, Vanderbilt University): https://www.popsci.com/scitech/article/2009-06/why-your-voice-sounds-different-recordings/
- ScienceDaily (2013), Hate the sound of your voice? Not really (Albright College): https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/09/130912112733.htm
- Hearing Review (2013), Study says we actually like our own voice: https://hearingreview.com/inside-hearing/research/study-says-we-actually-like-our-own-voice
- Discover Magazine (2021), Why the sound of your voice makes you cringe: https://www.discovermagazine.com/why-the-sound-of-your-voice-makes-you-cringe-42563

questions.q: Why does my voice sound different on recordings?
questions.a: When you talk, you hear your voice through the air and through vibrations in your skull, which boost the low frequencies. A recording only captures the air version, so it sounds thinner.

questions.q: Which voice is my real voice?
questions.a: The recorded one: it's the version everyone else hears.

questions.q: Why do people hate their recorded voice?
questions.a: It doesn't sound like the voice you're used to hearing in your head. In a 2013 study, people who didn't know their own voice was mixed in actually rated it as more attractive.
